description: Where tech meets humanity, we make an impact
summary: ARES (Astronaut Route and Environment Survival) is an interactive web app that takes users from a rotating 3D Mars, with clickable moons Phobos and Deimos, down to Gale Crater. It layers NASA data (Mars Trek imagery, MOLA elevation, THEMIS thermal, Curiosity REMS weather) into one hyperlocal view, then plans a safe Marswalk route that avoids steep slopes and boulders while visiting science targets. A survival dashboard tracks oxygen, radiation and turnaround time, with emergency shelter routing. It matters because astronaut safety depends on integrating mission data at the scale of a single spacewalk.
details:
ARES starts with a rover landing video that fades into a spinning Mars. Click a moon (Phobos or Deimos) for fun facts, or click Mars to dive into Gale Crater, where Curiosity has been exploring for years. There you can switch between NASA layers: imagery, elevation, thermal data and real weather readings from Curiosity and Perseverance

Benefits and impact
NASA’s Mars data is mostly built for global views. We wanted to bring it down to the size of a single spacewalk, with safety right next to the route. We hope it helps students, the public and mission planners see the trade-offs between science, time and risk on the surface.

What we used
React, TypeScript, Three.js, OpenLayers and Python for the data work, with NASA’s Mars Trek tiles, Curiosity weather data and JPL Horizons for the moon orbits. We hosted it on Azure Static Web Apps and built it on regular laptops.

What makes it creative
It feels more like a survival guide than a map. You fly in from orbit

What we considered
Safety first, honest science (we labeled anything exaggerated or assumed, like moon size and walking speed), working offline, and crediting NASA and USGS for the data.
